# One Theorem, Two Worlds: How Minimal Elements Tame the Infinite

## A puzzle about lists that never end

Imagine you are handed an endless conveyor belt. On it, one after another, come mathematical objects — graphs, say, or exponent patterns, or electrical networks. The belt never stops. Your task sounds impossible: no matter what stream of objects arrives, you must guarantee that *somewhere down the line, one object is a simplified copy of an earlier one*.

At first this feels hopeless. Surely a clever adversary could design an infinite parade in which every object is stubbornly "incomparable" to all the others — a mathematical antichain marching forever. Yet in many of the most important settings, the adversary cannot win. The parade *must* eventually repeat a pattern, in the precise sense that some later object contains an earlier one as a shrunken-down piece.

Orders with this magical property are called **well-quasi-orders**, and they are one of the quiet powerhouses of modern mathematics. This article is about a single, compact idea that sits at the heart of the well-quasi-order phenomenon — an idea that simultaneously explains a celebrated result about networks and shapes (the theory of *forbidden minors*) and a foundational result about polynomials (Dickson's lemma, the seed of computer algebra). The two look like they belong to different universes. They are, it turns out, the same theorem wearing two costumes.

## The costume of graphs: forbidden shapes

Start with graphs — dots (vertices) joined by lines (edges). A **minor** of a graph is anything you can obtain by three simple moves: delete an edge, delete a vertex, or *contract* an edge (fuse its two endpoints into one, sliding the neighbors together). Contraction is the interesting move: it is how you "shrink" a network while preserving its large-scale connectivity.

Many natural properties of networks are *minor-closed*: if a graph has the property, so does every one of its minors. The most famous example is **planarity** — being drawable in the plane without edges crossing. Shrink a planar network and it stays planar. Now here is the classical miracle: planarity is captured by a tiny blacklist. A graph is planar **if and only if** it does not contain either of two specific small graphs as a minor — the complete graph on five vertices, $K_5$, and the complete bipartite graph $K_{3,3}$ (the "three houses, three utilities" graph). Two forbidden shapes, and the entire infinite world of planar networks is pinned down.

The astonishing generalization, proved by Robertson and Seymour across a legendary series of papers, is that this is not a lucky accident of planarity. **Every** minor-closed property of finite graphs — no matter how exotic — is characterized by a *finite* list of forbidden minors. There is always a finite blacklist. The reason is exactly the conveyor-belt property: finite graphs are well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation. No infinite antichain of graphs can exist, and that single fact forces every blacklist to be finite.

## The costume of polynomials: monomial staircases

Now switch universes entirely. Forget graphs; think of exponent vectors. A monomial like $x^3 y^2 z$ is recorded by its vector of exponents $(3, 2, 1)$. We say one exponent vector *divides* another if it is smaller in every coordinate — $(3,2,1)$ divides $(5,2,4)$ because $3 \le 5$, $2 \le 2$, $1 \le 4$. This is the coordinatewise order on $\mathbb{N}^k$.

A **monomial ideal** is a collection of monomials closed upward under this divisibility: if a monomial is in, every multiple of it is in too. Geometrically, the exponent vectors of a monomial ideal form an infinite "staircase region" in the positive quadrant. **Dickson's lemma** says something that every student of computer algebra relies on: every such staircase, however intricate, is generated by *finitely many* corner monomials. Pick the minimal exponent vectors — the inner corners of the staircase — and there are only finitely many of them, and they generate everything above.

Dickson's lemma is the reason Gröbner bases exist, the reason polynomial equations can be solved by computer, the reason the whole edifice of computational algebra does not collapse into infinite regress. And its engine is, once again, the conveyor belt: $\mathbb{N}^k$ is well-quasi-ordered by coordinatewise divisibility.

## The shared machine underneath

Here is the punchline that unifies the two costumes. Both the finite forbidden-minor list and the finite generating staircase are consequences of one abstract lemma about *any* well-quasi-order. Strip away graphs, strip away polynomials, and keep only an ordering with the conveyor-belt property. Then:

> **In any well-quasi-order, every upward-closed set is generated by its minimal elements, and there are only finitely many of them.**

Two ingredients make this work, and they are beautifully simple.

**Ingredient one: minimal elements form an antichain.** Take any set $U$ and look at its *minimal* members — those with nothing strictly smaller still inside $U$. No two minimal elements can be comparable, because if one were below another, the larger would not be minimal. So the minimal elements form an antichain — a set of mutually incomparable objects. But in a well-quasi-order, *every antichain is finite*. (An infinite antichain would be exactly the never-repeating parade that the conveyor-belt property forbids.) Therefore there are only finitely many minimal elements.

**Ingredient two: everything sits above a minimal element.** Because a well-quasi-order has no infinite strictly-descending chains, if you start at any element of $U$ and keep stepping down while staying inside $U$, you must halt — and where you halt is, by definition, a minimal element. So every member of $U$ dominates one of the finitely many minimal elements.

Put the two together and you have the whole theorem. An upward-closed set $U$ is exactly $\{x : g \le x \text{ for some minimal } g\}$, and the set of $g$'s is finite. That is *finite generation* in full generality.

The forbidden-minor statement is simply this lemma read in a mirror. A minor-closed family $S$ is a *downward*-closed set. Its complement — the "bad" objects — is upward-closed, so by the lemma it has a finite set of minimal elements. Those minimal bad objects are precisely the **forbidden minors**: an object is good (in $S$) if and only if none of the finitely many forbidden minors sits below it. Robertson–Seymour's finite blacklist and Dickson's finite staircase corners are the *same finite antichain of minimal elements*, viewed from opposite sides.

## Why the abstraction is the point

It is tempting to see "abstract nonsense" as a retreat from real mathematics. Here it is the opposite: the abstraction is where the explanatory power lives. Once you isolate the engine, you see that the choice between graphs and polynomials was never essential. Any structure carrying a well-quasi-ordered relation automatically inherits a finite-obstruction theorem. This is why the same pattern keeps reappearing:

- **Words and languages.** Higman's lemma says finite strings over a finite alphabet are well-quasi-ordered by the subsequence relation. Consequence: any language closed under taking subsequences is defined by finitely many forbidden patterns.
- **Trees.** Kruskal's tree theorem extends the conveyor-belt property to finite trees under topological embedding, again yielding finite obstruction sets.
- **Matroids.** Matroids are the combinatorial abstraction of "independence" — they generalize both graphs and vector configurations over a field. Here lies the current research frontier. Graphs correspond exactly to matroids representable over the two-element field, so Robertson–Seymour is really a statement about $\mathbb{F}_2$-representable matroids. Geelen, Gerards, and Whittle proved the sweeping generalization that matroids representable over **any** finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ are well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation. The moment that conveyor-belt property is in hand, the finite-obstruction machine described above delivers a finite list of excluded minors for representability — completely automatically.

The matroid story also comes with a cautionary edge that makes the abstraction sharper. The conveyor-belt property is *not* universal: the class of *all* matroids is **not** well-quasi-ordered — one can build genuine infinite antichains of matroids, none a minor of another. So the finite-blacklist conclusion genuinely fails there. This is the abstraction earning its keep: it tells you exactly which hypothesis is load-bearing (well-quasi-ordering) and exactly what breaks without it (finiteness of the obstruction set).

## A concrete taste: forbidden patterns on the number line

To see the machine turn with no moving parts hidden, run it on the simplest ordered world imaginable — the natural numbers $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$ under their usual order. This is trivially a well-quasi-order. A downward-closed set of numbers is just an initial segment: either all of $\mathbb{N}$, or $\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ for some cutoff $n$. The machine predicts a finite forbidden set. And indeed: the set $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ is described by the single forbidden element $n$ — a number is "allowed" precisely when $n$ is not $\le$ it. One forbidden minor, exactly as the theory promises. The whole of $\mathbb{N}$ needs an *empty* forbidden set. The abstract theorem and the hand computation agree perfectly, which is the reassuring sound of a general principle clicking into place.

Bump the dimension to $\mathbb{N}^k$ and the same machine reproduces Dickson's staircase corners; wrap it around the minor order on graphs and it reproduces the Robertson–Seymour blacklist. Same gears, different housings.

## The moral

Mathematics prizes moments when two long-separated cities turn out to share a subway line. The theory of forbidden minors — a jewel of structural graph theory, and the shape of a major open frontier in matroid theory — and Dickson's lemma — the bedrock of computational algebra — are joined by exactly such a line. The train that runs between them carries a single, almost humble cargo: *in a well-quasi-order, the minimal elements are finite, and they explain everything above them.*

Finitely many corners. Finitely many forbidden shapes. One idea, taming two infinities at once.

# A Well-Quasi-Order Finite-Basis Engine: Unifying Forbidden Minors and Dickson's Lemma

**Author:** Aristotle

**Date:** 2026-07-10

## Abstract

We isolate and prove a single order-theoretic principle that underlies two results usually presented in separate fields: the finite forbidden-minor characterization of minor-closed families (the structural-graph/matroid setting, exemplified by the Robertson–Seymour theorem and its conjectural extension to $\mathbb{F}_q$-representable matroids) and Dickson's lemma on the finite generation of monomial ideals (the commutative-algebra setting). The principle is elementary to state: *in any partial order that is well-quasi-ordered by $\le$, every upward-closed set is generated by its finitely many minimal elements, and dually every downward-closed set is cut out by the finitely many minimal elements of its complement.* We give complete proofs of the abstract statements, derive both classical corollaries as literal specializations, and record the concrete instantiation on the exponent lattice $\mathbb{N}^k$ (Dickson's lemma) and on $\mathbb{N}$ itself. The contribution is not a new hard theorem but a clean identification of the shared engine: the finiteness of the obstruction set is exactly the finiteness of an antichain in a well-quasi-order, and the generation property is exactly the well-foundedness of the strict order. We discuss how the deep inputs (Robertson–Seymour; the Geelen–Gerards–Whittle well-quasi-ordering of $\mathbb{F}_q$-representable matroids) plug into the engine as hypotheses, and we outline extensions to Higman's lemma, Kruskal's tree theorem, and effective decision procedures.

## 1. Introduction

Two finiteness theorems, discovered in different centuries and different subfields, share a strikingly similar shape.

The first is the **finite forbidden-minor** phenomenon. A family $\mathcal{S}$ of finite graphs is *minor-closed* if it is closed under deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges. The Robertson–Seymour theorem asserts that finite graphs are well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation, from which it follows that every minor-closed family is characterized by a **finite** set of forbidden minors: a graph belongs to $\mathcal{S}$ if and only if none of finitely many specified graphs is a minor of it. The canonical instance is Wagner's theorem: a graph is planar iff it has neither $K_5$ nor $K_{3,3}$ as a minor. Because finite graphs coincide with matroids representable over $\mathbb{F}_2$, this is the base case of a broad program in matroid theory: Geelen, Gerards, and Whittle proved that for every finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, the class of $\mathbb{F}_q$-representable matroids is well-quasi-ordered by the matroid minor relation, whence every minor-closed class of such matroids has a finite set of excluded minors.

The second is **Dickson's lemma**: the coordinatewise (divisibility) order on $\mathbb{N}^k$ is a well-quasi-order, and consequently every monomial ideal — equivalently, every upward-closed set of exponent vectors — is finitely generated. This is the combinatorial heart of the existence and termination of Gröbner bases, and hence of a large fraction of computer algebra.

Our purpose is to make explicit that both finiteness theorems are corollaries of one abstract lemma about well-quasi-orders, and to give complete, self-contained proofs of the abstract lemma and its two specializations. The technical crux is short:

1. The set of minimal elements of any subset of a partial order is an **antichain**.
2. In a well-quasi-order, every antichain is **finite**.
3. In a well-quasi-order, the strict order is **well-founded**, so every element of a set dominates a minimal element of that set.

Items (1)–(3) combine to yield finite generation of upper sets; reading the statement for the complement of a lower set yields the finite forbidden-obstruction characterization. We regard the identification and clean packaging of this engine — and the observation that the two named theorems are the *same* statement viewed from opposite sides of a complement — as the contribution.

## 2. Preliminaries: well-quasi-orders

Throughout, $\alpha$ is a set carrying a partial order $\le$, with associated strict order $<$ (so $x < y$ means $x \le y$ and $x \ne y$).

**Definition 2.1 (Well-quasi-order).** A relation $\le$ on $\alpha$ is a *well-quasi-order* (WQO) if it is reflexive and transitive and, for every infinite sequence $x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$ in $\alpha$, there exist indices $i < j$ with $x_i \le x_j$. Equivalently, $\le$ has neither an infinite strictly descending chain nor an infinite antichain.

We record the two consequences of Definition 2.1 that we use.

**Fact 2.2 (Antichains are finite).** If $\le$ is a WQO on $\alpha$ and $A \subseteq \alpha$ is an antichain (i.e. no two distinct elements of $A$ are $\le$-comparable), then $A$ is finite.

*Reason.* An infinite antichain would furnish an infinite sequence with no $i<j$ satisfying $x_i \le x_j$, contradicting Definition 2.1.

**Fact 2.3 (Well-foundedness of $<$).** If $\le$ is a WQO on $\alpha$, then the strict order $<$ is well-founded: there is no infinite strictly descending chain $x_0 > x_1 > x_2 > \cdots$, and every nonempty subset has a $<$-minimal element.

*Reason.* An infinite descending chain $x_0 > x_1 > \cdots$ would be an infinite sequence with $x_i \not\le x_j$ for all $i < j$ (since $x_j < x_i$ and the order is a partial order), again contradicting Definition 2.1.

**Definition 2.4 (Upper and lower sets).** A set $U \subseteq \alpha$ is an *upper set* (upward-closed) if $x \in U$ and $x \le y$ imply $y \in U$. A set $S \subseteq \alpha$ is a *lower set* (downward-closed) if $x \in S$ and $y \le x$ imply $y \in S$. The complement of an upper set is a lower set and vice versa.

## 3. The finite-basis engine

We fix a partial order $\alpha$ and a subset.

**Definition 3.1 (Minimal generators).** For $U \subseteq \alpha$, the set of *minimal elements* of $U$ is
$$\operatorname{Min}(U) = \{\, x \in U \;:\; \forall y,\ y < x \Rightarrow y \notin U \,\}.$$

Immediately $\operatorname{Min}(U) \subseteq U$.

**Lemma 3.2 (Minimal elements form an antichain).** For every $U \subseteq \alpha$, the set $\operatorname{Min}(U)$ is an antichain under $\le$.

*Proof.* Let $x, y \in \operatorname{Min}(U)$ be distinct and suppose $x \le y$. Then $x < y$ (as $x \ne y$). But $x \in U$ contradicts the minimality of $y$, which forbids any element of $U$ strictly below $y$. Hence no two distinct minimal elements are comparable. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 3.3 (Finiteness of the minimal set).** If $\le$ is a WQO on $\alpha$, then $\operatorname{Min}(U)$ is finite for every $U \subseteq \alpha$.

*Proof.* By Lemma 3.2, $\operatorname{Min}(U)$ is an antichain; by Fact 2.2, antichains in a WQO are finite. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 3.4 (Domination by a minimal element).** If $\le$ is a WQO on $\alpha$ and $x \in U$, then there exists $g \in \operatorname{Min}(U)$ with $g \le x$.

*Proof.* Consider the nonempty set $D = \{\, y \in U : y \le x \,\}$ (nonempty since $x \in D$). By Fact 2.3, $<$ is well-founded, so $D$ has a $<$-minimal element $g$: an element $g \in D$ such that no $z \in D$ satisfies $z < g$. We claim $g \in \operatorname{Min}(U)$. Indeed $g \in U$ and $g \le x$. If some $z < g$ had $z \in U$, then $z \le g \le x$ gives $z \in D$ and $z < g$, contradicting minimality of $g$ in $D$. Hence no element of $U$ lies strictly below $g$, i.e. $g \in \operatorname{Min}(U)$, and $g \le x$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Theorem 3.5 (Upper sets are generated by their minimal elements).** Let $\le$ be a WQO on $\alpha$ and let $U \subseteq \alpha$ be an upper set. Then for all $x \in \alpha$,
$$x \in U \iff \exists\, g \in \operatorname{Min}(U),\ g \le x.$$

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) This is Lemma 3.4. ($\Leftarrow$) If $g \in \operatorname{Min}(U) \subseteq U$ and $g \le x$, then $x \in U$ because $U$ is upward-closed. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Theorem 3.6 (Finite generation of upper sets).** Let $\le$ be a WQO on $\alpha$ and let $U \subseteq \alpha$ be an upper set. Then there is a **finite** set $G \subseteq U$ with
$$\forall x,\quad x \in U \iff \exists\, g \in G,\ g \le x.$$
One may take $G = \operatorname{Min}(U)$.

*Proof.* Take $G = \operatorname{Min}(U)$. It is a subset of $U$ (Definition 3.1), finite (Lemma 3.3), and generates $U$ (Theorem 3.5). $\qquad\blacksquare$

Theorem 3.6 is the abstract form of both Dickson's lemma and Higman's finite-basis property.

**Theorem 3.7 (Finite forbidden-obstruction characterization of lower sets).** Let $\le$ be a WQO on $\alpha$ and let $S \subseteq \alpha$ be a lower set. Then there is a **finite** set $B \subseteq S^{\mathsf c}$ with
$$\forall x,\quad x \in S \iff \forall\, b \in B,\ \neg\,(b \le x).$$
One may take $B = \operatorname{Min}(S^{\mathsf c})$, the minimal elements of the complement.

*Proof.* The complement $U = S^{\mathsf c}$ is an upper set (Definition 2.4). Apply Theorem 3.6 to $U$, obtaining a finite $B = \operatorname{Min}(U) \subseteq U = S^{\mathsf c}$ with $x \in S^{\mathsf c} \iff \exists b \in B,\ b \le x$. Negating both sides and using $x \in S \iff x \notin S^{\mathsf c}$ gives $x \in S \iff \neg\,\exists b \in B,\ b \le x$, i.e. $x \in S \iff \forall b \in B,\ \neg(b \le x)$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Corollary 3.8 (Abstract Robertson–Seymour).** Let a class of combinatorial objects be equipped with a "minor" partial order $\le$ that is a WQO. Then every minor-closed property (i.e. every lower set) $S$ is characterized by a *finite* family of forbidden minors: there is a finite set $\mathcal{F}$ with
$$x \in S \iff \text{no } b \in \mathcal{F} \text{ is a minor of } x.$$

*Proof.* This is Theorem 3.7, with $\mathcal{F} = B$ and "$b \le x$" read as "$b$ is a minor of $x$." $\qquad\blacksquare$

The two theorems 3.6 and 3.7 are logically equivalent (each is the other applied to the complementary set), a fact worth emphasizing: **finite generation of upper sets and finite forbidden-minor characterization of lower sets are one theorem.** The obstruction family in the Robertson–Seymour reading is literally the minimal-generator family in the Dickson reading, transported across a complement.

## 4. Concrete specializations

### 4.1 Dickson's lemma on $\mathbb{N}^k$

Endow $\mathbb{N}^k$ (equivalently, functions $\{1,\dots,k\} \to \mathbb{N}$) with the coordinatewise order: $a \le b$ iff $a_i \le b_i$ for all $i$. Under the correspondence "exponent vector $\leftrightarrow$ monomial," this order is monomial divisibility, and upper sets are precisely the exponent sets of monomial ideals.

**Fact 4.1 (Dickson, WQO form).** The coordinatewise order on $\mathbb{N}^k$ is a well-quasi-order.

This is the classical statement of Dickson's lemma; it follows from the WQO property of $(\mathbb{N}, \le)$ by the general fact that a finite product of WQOs is a WQO. Feeding Fact 4.1 into Theorem 3.6 yields the finite-generation reading.

**Theorem 4.2 (Dickson, finite-generation form).** Every upward-closed set $U \subseteq \mathbb{N}^k$ is finitely generated: there is a finite $G \subseteq U$ with $x \in U \iff \exists g \in G,\ g \le x$. Equivalently, every monomial ideal is generated by finitely many monomials, namely those corresponding to the minimal exponent vectors of $U$.

*Proof.* Immediate from Theorem 3.6 and Fact 4.1. $\qquad\blacksquare$

This is exactly the finiteness result on which the theory of Gröbner bases rests: the minimal exponent vectors are the exponents of a minimal monomial generating set, and their finiteness underwrites the termination of Buchberger-type algorithms.

### 4.2 Initial segments of $\mathbb{N}$

The simplest nontrivial instance is $\alpha = \mathbb{N}$ with its usual (total, well-founded) order, which is a WQO.

**Theorem 4.3 (Forbidden set on $\mathbb{N}$).** Every lower set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is cut out by a finite forbidden set: there is a finite $B$ with $x \in S \iff \forall b \in B,\ \neg(b \le x)$.

*Proof.* Immediate from Theorem 3.7 and the WQO property of $(\mathbb{N},\le)$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Concretely, the lower sets of $\mathbb{N}$ are the initial segments. If $S = \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$, then $S^{\mathsf c} = \{n, n+1, \dots\}$ has the single minimal element $n$, so $B = \{n\}$: a number is in $S$ iff $n \not\le$ it. If $S = \mathbb{N}$, then $S^{\mathsf c} = \varnothing$ and $B = \varnothing$. The abstract prediction of a finite forbidden set matches the elementary computation exactly — a sanity check that the engine turns correctly at the ground floor.

### 4.3 The matroid frontier

The mission theme is the extension of the forbidden-minor phenomenon from graphs to matroids representable over a finite field. Two structural inputs sit above the engine of Section 3:

- **Base case ($\mathbb{F}_2$).** Finite graphs are the matroids representable over the two-element field, and the Robertson–Seymour theorem provides the WQO hypothesis for the graph minor order. Corollary 3.8 then yields the finite forbidden-minor characterization of every minor-closed graph property.
- **General finite fields ($\mathbb{F}_q$).** Geelen, Gerards, and Whittle established that $\mathbb{F}_q$-representable matroids are well-quasi-ordered by the matroid minor relation. Corollary 3.8 again applies, giving a finite excluded-minor set for every minor-closed class of $\mathbb{F}_q$-representable matroids — in particular a finite excluded-minor characterization of $\mathbb{F}_q$-representability itself. For the ternary field $\mathbb{F}_3$, the excluded minors for representability are known to be a finite explicit list (including the Fano matroid $F_7$, its dual $F_7^{*}$, and the non-Pappus matroid), consistent with the general theorem.

The engine also delineates a genuine boundary. The class of **all** matroids is *not* well-quasi-ordered — infinite antichains of matroids exist — so the finiteness conclusion legitimately fails there. This shows the WQO hypothesis in Corollary 3.8 is not removable: it is exactly the property that guarantees finite antichains and hence a finite obstruction set.

## 5. Algorithmic reading

Beyond existence, Theorems 3.6–3.7 organize a decision-procedure schema for membership in a minor-closed (lower) set $S$, given:

1. a finite obstruction family $B$ (which the theorems guarantee exists), and
2. a decidable test for the relation $b \le x$ ("is $b$ a minor of $x$?").

Then membership $x \in S$ is decided by checking, for each $b \in B$, whether $b \le x$, and answering "yes" iff all checks fail. The correctness is exactly Theorem 3.7. Two comments:

- The obstruction family $B = \operatorname{Min}(S^{\mathsf c})$ is guaranteed finite but the proof is non-constructive in general: WQO gives finiteness of the antichain, not an a priori bound on its size or a way to enumerate it. Making $B$ effective is a separate problem, solved case-by-case (e.g. Wagner's two obstructions for planarity, or the explicit list for $\mathbb{F}_3$-representability).
- On the Dickson side the schema becomes the familiar membership test for a monomial ideal: a monomial lies in the ideal iff it is divisible by one of the finitely many minimal generators. This is a routine, fully effective check once the generators are known, and it is the primitive operation inside Gröbner-basis reduction.

We give runnable illustrations of both readings — finite generation of a monomial ideal and finite-obstruction membership testing — in the accompanying numerical demonstration.

## 6. Discussion

The value of isolating the engine is threefold.

**Explanatory unification.** Dickson's lemma and the Robertson–Seymour finite-obstruction corollary are not merely analogous; they are the *same* order-theoretic statement, one about an upper set and one about the complement of a lower set. The finite basis of a monomial ideal and the finite blacklist of forbidden minors are the same finite antichain of minimal elements.

**Hypothesis isolation.** The engine cleanly separates the *easy* order theory (finiteness of antichains, well-foundedness of the strict order) from the *hard* structural input (that a given class is actually a WQO). All the depth of Robertson–Seymour and Geelen–Gerards–Whittle is concentrated in verifying the WQO hypothesis; once that is granted, the finite-obstruction corollary is elementary.

**Reusability.** Because the engine is stated for an arbitrary WQO, any future WQO theorem immediately yields a finite-obstruction corollary. Higman's lemma (finite words under the subsequence order) and Kruskal's tree theorem (finite trees under topological embedding) are the standard next inputs, each producing finite forbidden-pattern characterizations of subword-closed languages and tree-minor-closed families respectively.

## 7. Future directions

- **An explicit matroid minor order.** Build a partial order on isomorphism classes of matroids from the minor relation so that the abstract Robertson–Seymour corollary applies literally to matroids; the WQO input remains a hypothesis, but the forbidden-minor conclusion becomes a genuine matroid statement.
- **The graph-minor order.** Equip finite graphs (up to isomorphism) with the minor order and derive the finite forbidden-minor characterization of any minor-closed graph property, given the Robertson–Seymour WQO hypothesis.
- **Dickson to Hilbert.** Connect the finite generating set produced here to monomial ideals proper, showing the minimal-generator set is an actual generating set of the ideal, recovering finite generation and linking to Gröbner-basis infrastructure.
- **Higman's lemma.** Extend from finite products $\mathbb{N}^k$ to finite words over a WQO alphabet, yielding finite obstruction sets for subword-closed languages.
- **Kruskal's tree theorem.** Use tree embedding as a further WQO input, feeding the same finite-obstruction corollary for tree-minor-closed families.
- **Effective/decidable versions.** For decidable minor tests and finite ambient data, refine the abstract finite obstruction set into a concrete finite list, yielding a decision-procedure schema for membership in a minor-closed class.

## 8. Conclusion

A single lemma — *in a well-quasi-order, every upper set is generated by its finite antichain of minimal elements* — subsumes both the finite generation of monomial ideals (Dickson's lemma) and the finite forbidden-minor characterization of minor-closed families (the Robertson–Seymour corollary, and its matroid extension over finite fields). The two celebrated theorems are one statement viewed from opposite sides of a set-complement. The engine also marks its own limits: without the well-quasi-ordering hypothesis, as for the class of all matroids, the finiteness conclusion fails. Identifying and cleanly proving this shared engine is a small piece of unification with outsized reach across combinatorics and algebra.

\title{A Well-Quasi-Order Finite-Basis Engine:\\ Unifying Forbidden Minors and Dickson's Lemma}
\author{Aristotle}
\date{2026-07-10}

\begin{document}

\begin{abstract}
We isolate and prove a single order-theoretic principle that underlies two results
usually presented in separate fields: the finite forbidden-minor characterization of
minor-closed families (the structural-graph/matroid setting, exemplified by the
Robertson--Seymour theorem and its conjectural extension to $\FF_q$-representable
matroids) and Dickson's lemma on the finite generation of monomial ideals (the
commutative-algebra setting). The principle is elementary to state: \emph{in any partial
order that is well-quasi-ordered by $\le$, every upward-closed set is generated by its
finitely many minimal elements, and dually every downward-closed set is cut out by the
finitely many minimal elements of its complement.} We give complete proofs of the
abstract statements, derive both classical corollaries as literal specializations, and
record the concrete instantiation on the exponent lattice $\NN^k$ (Dickson's lemma) and on
$\NN$ itself. The contribution is a clean identification of the shared engine: the
finiteness of the obstruction set is exactly the finiteness of an antichain in a
well-quasi-order, and the generation property is exactly the well-foundedness of the strict
order. We discuss how the deep inputs (Robertson--Seymour; the Geelen--Gerards--Whittle
well-quasi-ordering of $\FF_q$-representable matroids) plug into the engine as hypotheses,
and we outline extensions to Higman's lemma, Kruskal's tree theorem, and effective decision
procedures.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}

Two finiteness theorems, discovered in different centuries and different subfields, share a
strikingly similar shape.

The first is the \emph{finite forbidden-minor} phenomenon. A family $\mathcal{S}$ of finite
graphs is \emph{minor-closed} if it is closed under deleting vertices and edges and
contracting edges. The Robertson--Seymour theorem asserts that finite graphs are
well-quasi-ordered by the minor relation, from which it follows that every minor-closed
family is characterized by a \textbf{finite} set of forbidden minors: a graph belongs to
$\mathcal{S}$ if and only if none of finitely many specified graphs is a minor of it. The
canonical instance is Wagner's theorem: a graph is planar iff it has neither $K_5$ nor
$K_{3,3}$ as a minor. Because finite graphs coincide with matroids representable over
$\FF_2$, this is the base case of a broad program in matroid theory: Geelen, Gerards, and
Whittle proved that for every finite field $\FF_q$, the class of $\FF_q$-representable
matroids is well-quasi-ordered by the matroid minor relation, whence every minor-closed
class of such matroids has a finite set of excluded minors.

The second is \emph{Dickson's lemma}: the coordinatewise (divisibility) order on $\NN^k$ is
a well-quasi-order, and consequently every monomial ideal --- equivalently, every
upward-closed set of exponent vectors --- is finitely generated. This is the combinatorial
heart of the existence and termination of Gr\"obner bases, and hence of a large fraction of
computer algebra.

Our purpose is to make explicit that both finiteness theorems are corollaries of one
abstract lemma about well-quasi-orders, and to give complete, self-contained proofs of the
abstract lemma and its two specializations. The technical crux is short:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The set of minimal elements of any subset of a partial order is an \textbf{antichain}.
\item In a well-quasi-order, every antichain is \textbf{finite}.
\item In a well-quasi-order, the strict order is \textbf{well-founded}, so every element of a
set dominates a minimal element of that set.
\end{enumerate}
Items (1)--(3) combine to yield finite generation of upper sets; reading the statement for
the complement of a lower set yields the finite forbidden-obstruction characterization. We
regard the identification and clean packaging of this engine --- and the observation that
the two named theorems are the \emph{same} statement viewed from opposite sides of a
complement --- as the contribution.

\section{Preliminaries: well-quasi-orders}

Throughout, $\alpha$ is a set carrying a partial order $\le$, with associated strict order
$<$ (so $x < y$ means $x \le y$ and $x \ne y$).

\begin{definition}[Well-quasi-order]
A relation $\le$ on $\alpha$ is a \emph{well-quasi-order} (WQO) if it is reflexive and
transitive and, for every infinite sequence $x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$ in $\alpha$, there exist
indices $i < j$ with $x_i \le x_j$. Equivalently, $\le$ has neither an infinite strictly
descending chain nor an infinite antichain.
\end{definition}

\begin{fact}[Antichains are finite]\label{fact:antichain}
If $\le$ is a WQO on $\alpha$ and $A \subseteq \alpha$ is an antichain (no two distinct
elements of $A$ are $\le$-comparable), then $A$ is finite.
\end{fact}

\begin{proof}
An infinite antichain would furnish an infinite sequence with no $i<j$ satisfying
$x_i \le x_j$, contradicting the definition of WQO.
\end{proof}

\begin{fact}[Well-foundedness of $<$]\label{fact:wf}
If $\le$ is a WQO on $\alpha$, then the strict order $<$ is well-founded: there is no
infinite strictly descending chain, and every nonempty subset has a $<$-minimal element.
\end{fact}

\begin{proof}
An infinite descending chain $x_0 > x_1 > \cdots$ would be an infinite sequence with
$x_i \not\le x_j$ for all $i < j$, again contradicting the definition of WQO.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Upper and lower sets]
A set $U \subseteq \alpha$ is an \emph{upper set} (upward-closed) if $x \in U$ and
$x \le y$ imply $y \in U$. A set $S \subseteq \alpha$ is a \emph{lower set}
(downward-closed) if $x \in S$ and $y \le x$ imply $y \in S$. The complement of an upper set
is a lower set and vice versa.
\end{definition}

\section{The finite-basis engine}

\begin{definition}[Minimal generators]
For $U \subseteq \alpha$, the set of \emph{minimal elements} of $U$ is
\[
\Min(U) = \{\, x \in U \;:\; \forall y,\ y < x \Rightarrow y \notin U \,\}.
\]
\end{definition}

Immediately $\Min(U) \subseteq U$.

\begin{lemma}[Minimal elements form an antichain]\label{lem:antichain}
For every $U \subseteq \alpha$, the set $\Min(U)$ is an antichain under $\le$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $x, y \in \Min(U)$ be distinct and suppose $x \le y$. Then $x < y$ (as $x \ne y$). But
$x \in U$ contradicts the minimality of $y$, which forbids any element of $U$ strictly below
$y$. Hence no two distinct minimal elements are comparable.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finiteness of the minimal set]\label{lem:finite}
If $\le$ is a WQO on $\alpha$, then $\Min(U)$ is finite for every $U \subseteq \alpha$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:antichain}, $\Min(U)$ is an antichain; by Fact~\ref{fact:antichain},
antichains in a WQO are finite.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Domination by a minimal element]\label{lem:dom}
If $\le$ is a WQO on $\alpha$ and $x \in U$, then there exists $g \in \Min(U)$ with
$g \le x$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Consider the nonempty set $D = \{\, y \in U : y \le x \,\}$ (nonempty since $x \in D$). By
Fact~\ref{fact:wf}, $<$ is well-founded, so $D$ has a $<$-minimal element $g$: an element
$g \in D$ such that no $z \in D$ satisfies $z < g$. We claim $g \in \Min(U)$. Indeed
$g \in U$ and $g \le x$. If some $z < g$ had $z \in U$, then $z \le g \le x$ gives $z \in D$
and $z < g$, contradicting minimality of $g$ in $D$. Hence no element of $U$ lies strictly
below $g$, i.e.\ $g \in \Min(U)$, and $g \le x$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Upper sets are generated by their minimal elements]\label{thm:gen}
Let $\le$ be a WQO on $\alpha$ and let $U \subseteq \alpha$ be an upper set. Then for all
$x \in \alpha$,
\[
x \in U \iff \exists\, g \in \Min(U),\ g \le x.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) This is Lemma~\ref{lem:dom}. ($\Leftarrow$) If $g \in \Min(U) \subseteq U$
and $g \le x$, then $x \in U$ because $U$ is upward-closed.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite generation of upper sets]\label{thm:fingen}
Let $\le$ be a WQO on $\alpha$ and let $U \subseteq \alpha$ be an upper set. Then there is a
\textbf{finite} set $G \subseteq U$ with
\[
\forall x,\quad x \in U \iff \exists\, g \in G,\ g \le x.
\]
One may take $G = \Min(U)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $G = \Min(U)$. It is a subset of $U$, finite (Lemma~\ref{lem:finite}), and generates
$U$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:gen}).
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:fingen} is the abstract form of both Dickson's lemma and Higman's
finite-basis property.

\begin{theorem}[Finite forbidden-obstruction characterization of lower sets]\label{thm:forb}
Let $\le$ be a WQO on $\alpha$ and let $S \subseteq \alpha$ be a lower set. Then there is a
\textbf{finite} set $B \subseteq S^{\comp}$ with
\[
\forall x,\quad x \in S \iff \forall\, b \in B,\ \neg\,(b \le x).
\]
One may take $B = \Min(S^{\comp})$, the minimal elements of the complement.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The complement $U = S^{\comp}$ is an upper set. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:fingen} to $U$,
obtaining a finite $B = \Min(U) \subseteq U = S^{\comp}$ with
$x \in S^{\comp} \iff \exists b \in B,\ b \le x$. Negating both sides and using
$x \in S \iff x \notin S^{\comp}$ gives $x \in S \iff \neg\,\exists b \in B,\ b \le x$, i.e.\
$x \in S \iff \forall b \in B,\ \neg(b \le x)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Abstract Robertson--Seymour]\label{cor:rs}
Let a class of combinatorial objects be equipped with a ``minor'' partial order $\le$ that is
a WQO. Then every minor-closed property (i.e.\ every lower set) $S$ is characterized by a
\emph{finite} family of forbidden minors: there is a finite set $\mathcal{F}$ with
\[
x \in S \iff \text{no } b \in \mathcal{F} \text{ is a minor of } x.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
This is Theorem~\ref{thm:forb}, with $\mathcal{F} = B$ and ``$b \le x$'' read as ``$b$ is a
minor of $x$.''
\end{proof}

Theorems~\ref{thm:fingen} and~\ref{thm:forb} are logically equivalent (each is the other
applied to the complementary set): \textbf{finite generation of upper sets and finite
forbidden-minor characterization of lower sets are one theorem.} The obstruction family in
the Robertson--Seymour reading is literally the minimal-generator family in the Dickson
reading, transported across a complement.

\section{Concrete specializations}

\subsection{Dickson's lemma on $\NN^k$}

Endow $\NN^k$ with the coordinatewise order: $a \le b$ iff $a_i \le b_i$ for all $i$. Under
the correspondence ``exponent vector $\leftrightarrow$ monomial,'' this order is monomial
divisibility, and upper sets are precisely the exponent sets of monomial ideals.

\begin{fact}[Dickson, WQO form]\label{fact:dickson}
The coordinatewise order on $\NN^k$ is a well-quasi-order.
\end{fact}

This follows from the WQO property of $(\NN, \le)$ and the fact that a finite product of WQOs
is a WQO.

\begin{theorem}[Dickson, finite-generation form]\label{thm:dickson}
Every upward-closed set $U \subseteq \NN^k$ is finitely generated: there is a finite
$G \subseteq U$ with $x \in U \iff \exists g \in G,\ g \le x$. Equivalently, every monomial
ideal is generated by finitely many monomials, namely those corresponding to the minimal
exponent vectors of $U$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:fingen} and Fact~\ref{fact:dickson}.
\end{proof}

This is exactly the finiteness result on which the theory of Gr\"obner bases rests: the
minimal exponent vectors are the exponents of a minimal monomial generating set, and their
finiteness underwrites the termination of Buchberger-type algorithms.

\subsection{Initial segments of $\NN$}

The simplest nontrivial instance is $\alpha = \NN$ with its usual (total, well-founded)
order, which is a WQO.

\begin{theorem}[Forbidden set on $\NN$]\label{thm:nat}
Every lower set $S \subseteq \NN$ is cut out by a finite forbidden set: there is a finite $B$
with $x \in S \iff \forall b \in B,\ \neg(b \le x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:forb} and the WQO property of $(\NN,\le)$.
\end{proof}

Concretely, if $S = \{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$, then $S^{\comp} = \{n, n+1, \dots\}$ has the single
minimal element $n$, so $B = \{n\}$: a number is in $S$ iff $n \not\le$ it. If $S = \NN$, then
$S^{\comp} = \varnothing$ and $B = \varnothing$. The abstract prediction of a finite
forbidden set matches the elementary computation exactly.

\subsection{The matroid frontier}

The extension of the forbidden-minor phenomenon from graphs to matroids representable over a
finite field rests on two structural inputs above the engine of Section~3:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Base case ($\FF_2$).} Finite graphs are the matroids representable over the
two-element field, and the Robertson--Seymour theorem provides the WQO hypothesis for the
graph minor order. Corollary~\ref{cor:rs} then yields the finite forbidden-minor
characterization of every minor-closed graph property.
\item \textbf{General finite fields ($\FF_q$).} Geelen, Gerards, and Whittle established that
$\FF_q$-representable matroids are well-quasi-ordered by the matroid minor relation.
Corollary~\ref{cor:rs} again applies, giving a finite excluded-minor set for every
minor-closed class of $\FF_q$-representable matroids --- in particular a finite excluded-minor
characterization of $\FF_q$-representability itself. For the ternary field $\FF_3$, the
excluded minors for representability form a finite explicit list (including the Fano matroid
$F_7$, its dual $F_7^{*}$, and the non-Pappus matroid).
\end{itemize}
The engine also delineates a genuine boundary. The class of \textbf{all} matroids is
\emph{not} well-quasi-ordered --- infinite antichains of matroids exist --- so the finiteness
conclusion legitimately fails there. This shows the WQO hypothesis in
Corollary~\ref{cor:rs} is not removable.

\section{Algorithmic reading}

Theorems~\ref{thm:fingen}--\ref{thm:forb} organize a decision-procedure schema for
membership in a minor-closed (lower) set $S$, given: (1) a finite obstruction family $B$
(guaranteed to exist), and (2) a decidable test for the relation $b \le x$. Then membership
$x \in S$ is decided by checking, for each $b \in B$, whether $b \le x$, and answering
``yes'' iff all checks fail; correctness is exactly Theorem~\ref{thm:forb}. The obstruction
family $B = \Min(S^{\comp})$ is guaranteed finite but the proof is non-constructive in
general: WQO gives finiteness of the antichain, not an a priori bound on its size or a way to
enumerate it. On the Dickson side the schema becomes the familiar membership test for a
monomial ideal: a monomial lies in the ideal iff it is divisible by one of the finitely many
minimal generators.

\section{Discussion}

The value of isolating the engine is threefold. \emph{Explanatory unification}: Dickson's
lemma and the Robertson--Seymour finite-obstruction corollary are the \emph{same}
order-theoretic statement, one about an upper set and one about the complement of a lower set.
\emph{Hypothesis isolation}: the engine separates the easy order theory (finiteness of
antichains, well-foundedness of the strict order) from the hard structural input (that a
given class is actually a WQO). \emph{Reusability}: any future WQO theorem immediately yields
a finite-obstruction corollary; Higman's lemma and Kruskal's tree theorem are the standard
next inputs.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{An explicit matroid minor order.} Build a partial order on isomorphism classes
of matroids from the minor relation so that the abstract Robertson--Seymour corollary applies
literally to matroids.
\item \textbf{The graph-minor order.} Equip finite graphs (up to isomorphism) with the minor
order and derive the finite forbidden-minor characterization of any minor-closed graph
property, given the Robertson--Seymour WQO hypothesis.
\item \textbf{Dickson to Hilbert.} Connect the finite generating set produced here to
monomial ideals proper, recovering finite generation and linking to Gr\"obner-basis
infrastructure.
\item \textbf{Higman's lemma.} Extend from finite products $\NN^k$ to finite words over a WQO
alphabet, yielding finite obstruction sets for subword-closed languages.
\item \textbf{Kruskal's tree theorem.} Use tree embedding as a further WQO input, feeding the
same finite-obstruction corollary for tree-minor-closed families.
\item \textbf{Effective/decidable versions.} For decidable minor tests and finite ambient
data, refine the abstract finite obstruction set into a concrete finite list, yielding a
decision-procedure schema for membership in a minor-closed class.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

A single lemma --- \emph{in a well-quasi-order, every upper set is generated by its finite
antichain of minimal elements} --- subsumes both the finite generation of monomial ideals
(Dickson's lemma) and the finite forbidden-minor characterization of minor-closed families
(the Robertson--Seymour corollary, and its matroid extension over finite fields). The two
celebrated theorems are one statement viewed from opposite sides of a set-complement. The
engine also marks its own limits: without the well-quasi-ordering hypothesis, as for the
class of all matroids, the finiteness conclusion fails.

"""
Numerical demonstrations of the well-quasi-order finite-basis engine.

Central principle (proved in the accompanying paper):

    In any well-quasi-order (WQO), every upward-closed set U is generated by
    its FINITELY many minimal elements Min(U):

        x in U  <=>  exists g in Min(U) with g <= x.

    Dually, every downward-closed (minor-closed) set S is cut out by the
    finitely many minimal elements of its complement -- the "forbidden set":

        x in S  <=>  for all b in B, not (b <= x).

This file specializes the principle to two concrete well-quasi-orders:

  * (N, <=)          -- initial segments and single forbidden numbers.
  * (N^k, <=coord)   -- Dickson's lemma: monomial ideals are finitely generated.

Everything is self-contained (standard library only) and type-hinted.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# A point of N^k is represented as a tuple of nonnegative ints.
Vec = Tuple[int, ...]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Coordinatewise order on N^k (= monomial divisibility)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def leq_coord(a: Vec, b: Vec) -> bool:
    """Return True iff a <= b coordinatewise (equivalently, monomial a divides b)."""
    return len(a) == len(b) and all(ai <= bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b))


def lt_coord(a: Vec, b: Vec) -> bool:
    """Strict coordinatewise order: a <= b and a != b."""
    return leq_coord(a, b) and a != b


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The abstract engine, made concrete for a finite sample of a set.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def minimal_elements(
    points: Iterable[Vec], leq: Callable[[Vec, Vec], bool]
) -> List[Vec]:
    """
    Compute the minimal elements Min(points) with respect to the order `leq`.

    An element x is minimal if no *distinct* element y of the set satisfies y < x.
    In a WQO this set is guaranteed finite; here `points` is already finite so we
    simply filter.
    """
    pts: List[Vec] = list(dict.fromkeys(points))  # dedupe, keep order
    result: List[Vec] = []
    for x in pts:
        if not any(y != x and leq(y, x) for y in pts):
            result.append(x)
    return sorted(result)


def generated_upper_set(
    generators: Sequence[Vec], box: int, dim: int
) -> Set[Vec]:
    """
    The upper set generated by `generators`, intersected with the finite box
    {0, ..., box}^dim.  A vector x is in the set iff some generator divides it.
    """
    out: Set[Vec] = set()
    for x in product(range(box + 1), repeat=dim):
        if any(leq_coord(g, x) for g in generators):
            out.add(x)
    return out


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 1: Dickson's lemma / monomial-ideal finite generation on N^2.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def demo_dickson_finite_generation() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("DEMO 1: Dickson's lemma -- finite generation of a monomial ideal")
    print("=" * 70)

    # Build an upper set U in N^2 as the divisibility-up-closure of a *redundant*
    # generating list.  The engine predicts a unique finite minimal generating
    # set Min(U); redundant generators should be pruned automatically.
    box, dim = 8, 2
    redundant_gens: List[Vec] = [
        (2, 3),  # minimal
        (4, 1),  # minimal
        (1, 5),  # minimal
        (5, 6),  # redundant: divisible by (2,3)
        (4, 4),  # redundant: divisible by (4,1)
        (3, 7),  # redundant: divisible by (1,5)
    ]
    U = generated_upper_set(redundant_gens, box, dim)
    mins = minimal_elements(U, leq_coord)

    print(f"Redundant generator list : {redundant_gens}")
    print(f"Minimal generators Min(U): {mins}")
    print(f"|U cap box|              : {len(U)} vectors in {{0..{box}}}^2")

    # Verify the generation identity on the whole box:
    #   x in U  <=>  some minimal generator divides x.
    ok = all(
        (x in U) == any(leq_coord(g, x) for g in mins)
        for x in product(range(box + 1), repeat=dim)
    )
    print(f"Generation identity holds on the box: {ok}")
    print(f"Minimal set is finite (as WQO guarantees): {len(mins)} elements")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 2: forbidden-set characterization of a lower set in N.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def forbidden_set_nat(in_S: Callable[[int], bool], bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """
    Given a lower set S of naturals (via membership test `in_S`) sampled on
    {0, ..., bound}, return the finite forbidden set B = Min(complement).
    """
    complement = [(n,) for n in range(bound + 1) if not in_S(n)]
    # minimal elements of complement under the usual order = least excluded number
    return [t[0] for t in minimal_elements(complement, leq_coord)]


def demo_forbidden_set_nat() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("DEMO 2: forbidden set of an initial segment of N")
    print("=" * 70)

    bound = 20
    for n in (0, 1, 5, 12):
        # S = {0, ..., n-1} is a lower set.
        in_S = lambda x, n=n: x < n
        B = forbidden_set_nat(in_S, bound)
        # Reconstruct S from B: x in S iff no b in B has b <= x.
        reconstructed = [x for x in range(bound + 1) if all(not (b <= x) for b in B)]
        expected = [x for x in range(bound + 1) if in_S(x)]
        print(
            f"S = {{0..{n-1}}}: forbidden set B = {B}; "
            f"reconstruction correct = {reconstructed == expected}"
        )
    # S = all of N (on the sample): empty forbidden set.
    B_all = forbidden_set_nat(lambda x: True, bound)
    print(f"S = N (sampled): forbidden set B = {B_all} (empty, as predicted)")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 3: membership decision via a finite obstruction family.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def decides_membership(x: Vec, forbidden: Sequence[Vec]) -> bool:
    """
    Decide membership of x in a minor-closed set S given its finite forbidden
    family: x in S iff no forbidden obstruction divides (is <= to) x.
    """
    return not any(leq_coord(b, x) for b in forbidden)


def demo_obstruction_membership() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("DEMO 3: minor-closed membership via a finite forbidden family (N^2)")
    print("=" * 70)

    # Take S = downward-closed set avoiding any vector that is >= a forbidden one.
    # Forbidden family (two obstructions), analogous to Wagner's {K5, K3,3}.
    forbidden: List[Vec] = [(2, 2), (0, 4)]
    print(f"Forbidden family (obstructions): {forbidden}")
    tests: List[Vec] = [(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 0), (1, 4), (0, 3), (2, 1)]
    for x in tests:
        verdict = decides_membership(x, forbidden)
        print(f"  x = {x}:  in S = {verdict}")

    # Cross-check that S really is downward closed on a box.
    box = 6
    S = {x for x in product(range(box + 1), repeat=2) if decides_membership(x, forbidden)}
    downward_closed = all(
        (y in S)
        for x in S
        for y in product(range(box + 1), repeat=2)
        if leq_coord(y, x)
    )
    print(f"S is downward-closed on {{0..{box}}}^2: {downward_closed}")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    demo_dickson_finite_generation()
    demo_forbidden_set_nat()
    demo_obstruction_membership()
    print("All demonstrations complete.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# A point of N^k is represented as a tuple of nonnegative ints.
Vec = Tuple[int, ...]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Coordinatewise order on N^k (= monomial divisibility)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def leq_coord(a: Vec, b: Vec) -> bool:
    """Return True iff a <= b coordinatewise (equivalently, monomial a divides b)."""
    return len(a) == len(b) and all(ai <= bi for ai, bi in zip(a, b))


def lt_coord(a: Vec, b: Vec) -> bool:
    """Strict coordinatewise order: a <= b and a != b."""
    return leq_coord(a, b) and a != b


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The abstract engine, made concrete for a finite sample of a set.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def minimal_elements(
    points: Iterable[Vec], leq: Callable[[Vec, Vec], bool]
) -> List[Vec]:
    """
    Compute the minimal elements Min(points) with respect to the order `leq`.

    An element x is minimal if no *distinct* element y of the set satisfies y < x.
    In a WQO this set is guaranteed finite; here `points` is already finite so we
    simply filter.
    """
    pts: List[Vec] = list(dict.fromkeys(points))  # dedupe, keep order
    result: List[Vec] = []
    for x in pts:
        if not any(y != x and leq(y, x) for y in pts):
            result.append(x)
    return sorted(result)


def generated_upper_set(
    generators: Sequence[Vec], box: int, dim: int
) -> Set[Vec]:
    """
    The upper set generated by `generators`, intersected with the finite box
    {0, ..., box}^dim.  A vector x is in the set iff some generator divides it.
    """
    out: Set[Vec] = set()
    for x in product(range(box + 1), repeat=dim):
        if any(leq_coord(g, x) for g in generators):
            out.add(x)
    return out


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 1: Dickson's lemma / monomial-ideal finite generation on N^2.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def demo_dickson_finite_generation() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("DEMO 1: Dickson's lemma -- finite generation of a monomial ideal")
    print("=" * 70)

    # Build an upper set U in N^2 as the divisibility-up-closure of a *redundant*
    # generating list.  The engine predicts a unique finite minimal generating
    # set Min(U); redundant generators should be pruned automatically.
    box, dim = 8, 2
    redundant_gens: List[Vec] = [
        (2, 3),  # minimal
        (4, 1),  # minimal
        (1, 5),  # minimal
        (5, 6),  # redundant: divisible by (2,3)
        (4, 4),  # redundant: divisible by (4,1)
        (3, 7),  # redundant: divisible by (1,5)
    ]
    U = generated_upper_set(redundant_gens, box, dim)
    mins = minimal_elements(U, leq_coord)

    print(f"Redundant generator list : {redundant_gens}")
    print(f"Minimal generators Min(U): {mins}")
    print(f"|U cap box|              : {len(U)} vectors in {{0..{box}}}^2")

    # Verify the generation identity on the whole box:
    #   x in U  <=>  some minimal generator divides x.
    ok = all(
        (x in U) == any(leq_coord(g, x) for g in mins)
        for x in product(range(box + 1), repeat=dim)
    )
    print(f"Generation identity holds on the box: {ok}")
    print(f"Minimal set is finite (as WQO guarantees): {len(mins)} elements")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 2: forbidden-set characterization of a lower set in N.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def forbidden_set_nat(in_S: Callable[[int], bool], bound: int) -> List[int]:
    """
    Given a lower set S of naturals (via membership test `in_S`) sampled on
    {0, ..., bound}, return the finite forbidden set B = Min(complement).
    """
    complement = [(n,) for n in range(bound + 1) if not in_S(n)]
    # minimal elements of complement under the usual order = least excluded number
    return [t[0] for t in minimal_elements(complement, leq_coord)]


def demo_forbidden_set_nat() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("DEMO 2: forbidden set of an initial segment of N")
    print("=" * 70)

    bound = 20
    for n in (0, 1, 5, 12):
        # S = {0, ..., n-1} is a lower set.
        in_S = lambda x, n=n: x < n
        B = forbidden_set_nat(in_S, bound)
        # Reconstruct S from B: x in S iff no b in B has b <= x.
        reconstructed = [x for x in range(bound + 1) if all(not (b <= x) for b in B)]
        expected = [x for x in range(bound + 1) if in_S(x)]
        print(
            f"S = {{0..{n-1}}}: forbidden set B = {B}; "
            f"reconstruction correct = {reconstructed == expected}"
        )
    # S = all of N (on the sample): empty forbidden set.
    B_all = forbidden_set_nat(lambda x: True, bound)
    print(f"S = N (sampled): forbidden set B = {B_all} (empty, as predicted)")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstration 3: membership decision via a finite obstruction family.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def decides_membership(x: Vec, forbidden: Sequence[Vec]) -> bool:
    """
    Decide membership of x in a minor-closed set S given its finite forbidden
    family: x in S iff no forbidden obstruction divides (is <= to) x.
    """
    return not any(leq_coord(b, x) for b in forbidden)

    print("DEMO 3: minor-closed membership via a finite forbidden family (N^2)")

        for x in S

        if leq_coord(y, x)
    )
    print(f"S is downward-closed on {{0..{box}}}^2: {downward_closed}")
    print()

    demo_dickson_finite_generation()
    demo_forbidden_set_nat()
    demo_obstruction_membership()
    print("All demonstrations complete.")

    main()

algorithms.name: Minimal-Element Extraction in a Well-Quasi-Order
algorithms.description: Given a finite sample of a set U in a partially ordered domain, compute the antichain Min(U) of its minimal elements. This is the constructive core of the finite-basis engine: in a well-quasi-order the full Min(U) is guaranteed finite and forms an antichain, so it doubles as the minimal generating set of an upper set (Dickson) and, applied to a complement, as the forbidden-minor family (Robertson-Seymour). Complexity is O(n^2 * c) for n sampled points and c the cost of one order comparison; a single pass compares each candidate against all others and keeps those with no strict predecessor in the set.

algorithms.name: Dickson Finite Generation of a Monomial Ideal
algorithms.description: Reduce a redundant list of monomial exponent vectors to the unique minimal generating set of the monomial ideal (equivalently, the upper set) they generate under coordinatewise divisibility on N^k. By Dickson's lemma the coordinatewise order is a well-quasi-order, so the minimal set is finite; this algorithm prunes every generator that is divisible by another. The output is the exponent set of a minimal monomial generating basis, the object whose finiteness underlies termination of Buchberger-style Groebner algorithms. Complexity O(m^2 * k) for m generators in dimension k.

algorithms.name: Forbidden-Obstruction Membership Decision
algorithms.description: Decide membership in a minor-closed (downward-closed) set S from a finite forbidden family B = Min(complement of S). The abstract Robertson-Seymour corollary guarantees such a finite B exists whenever the ambient order is a well-quasi-order; membership is then a bounded scan: x is in S iff no forbidden obstruction b satisfies b <= x. This mirrors Wagner's planarity test (forbid K5 and K3,3). Complexity O(|B| * c) per query, with c the cost of one minor/order test.

"""Visualize a monomial ideal (upper set) in N^2 and its minimal generators."""
from itertools import product
from typing import List, Tuple
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Vec = Tuple[int, int]

def divides(a: Vec, b: Vec) -> bool:
    return a[0] <= b[0] and a[1] <= b[1]

def main() -> None:
    box = 12
    gens: List[Vec] = [(2, 5), (4, 3), (7, 1), (1, 8)]
    U = [x for x in product(range(box + 1), repeat=2)
         if any(divides(g, x) for g in gens)]
    mins = [g for g in gens
            if not any(h != g and divides(h, g) for h in gens)]
    ux = [p[0] for p in U]; uy = [p[1] for p in U]
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6))
    plt.scatter(ux, uy, s=40, c="#7fb3d5", label="upper set U (ideal)")
    plt.scatter([m[0] for m in mins], [m[1] for m in mins],
                s=180, c="#c0392b", marker="*", label="minimal generators")

import Mathlib

/-!
# A well-quasi-order bridge: forbidden minors and Dickson's lemma

This file isolates and proves the *order-theoretic engine* that is shared by two
areas which, on the surface, look unrelated:

* **Structural graph / matroid theory.**  The Robertson–Seymour theorem asserts
  that finite graphs are *well-quasi-ordered* (WQO) by the minor relation.  Its
  headline corollary is that every minor-closed family of graphs is described by
  a **finite** set of forbidden minors.  The conjectural extension of
  Robertson–Seymour to the class of `F_q`-representable matroids (the mission
  theme) would, via the very same engine, give a finite set of *excluded minors*
  for every minor-closed family of representable matroids.

* **Commutative algebra.**  Dickson's lemma says that `ℕ^k` is well-quasi-ordered
  by the coordinatewise (divisibility) order.  Its headline corollary is that
  every monomial ideal — equivalently every upward-closed set of exponent
  vectors — is **finitely generated**.

Both corollaries are instances of one abstract fact:

> In *any* partial order that is well-quasi-ordered by `≤`, every upper set is
> generated by its (finitely many) minimal elements, and dually every lower set
> is cut out by the (finitely many) minimal elements of its complement.

The "finitely many" is the crucial point and is exactly where WQO is used: an
antichain in a WQO is finite (`IsAntichain.finite_of_wellQuasiOrdered`), and the
minimal elements of any set form an antichain.

## Main results

* `WQOFiniteBasis.mem_iff_exists_minimalGen` — an upper set is exactly the up-set
  generated by its minimal elements.
* `WQOFiniteBasis.exists_finite_generating_family` — **finite generation of upper
  sets** (the abstract Dickson / Higman statement).
* `WQOFiniteBasis.exists_finite_forbidden_family` — **finite forbidden-obstruction
  characterization** of lower sets (the abstract Robertson–Seymour statement).
* `WQOFiniteBasis.dickson` — concrete specialization to `Fin k → ℕ`: every
  monomial-ideal-shaped upper set is finitely generated.
* `WQOFiniteBasis.robertson_seymour_of_wqo` — the forbidden-minor corollary for
  any WQO "minor order" on an abstract class of combinatorial objects.

The WQO vocabulary (`WellQuasiOrdered`, `IsAntichain.finite_of_wellQuasiOrdered`,
`WellQuasiOrdered.wellFounded`, and the instance `WellQuasiOrderedLE (Fin k → ℕ)`)
is taken from `Mathlib.Order.WellQuasiOrder`; the *bridge* lemmas below —
generation of upper sets by minimal elements and the forbidden-obstruction
characterization of lower sets — are the new contribution.
-/

open Set

namespace WQOFiniteBasis

variable {α : Type*} [PartialOrder α]

/-- The set of `≤`-minimal elements of a set `U`. -/
def minimalGens (U : Set α) : Set α := {x | x ∈ U ∧ ∀ y, y < x → y ∉ U}

lemma minimalGens_subset (U : Set α) : minimalGens U ⊆ U := fun _ hx => hx.1

/-- Minimal elements of a set form an antichain. -/
lemma isAntichain_minimalGens (U : Set α) :
    IsAntichain (· ≤ ·) (minimalGens U) := by
  intro x hx y hy hxy
  exact fun h => hy.2 x (lt_of_le_of_ne h hxy) hx.1

/-- In a well-quasi-order, the set of minimal elements of any set is finite:
it is an antichain, and antichains are finite in a WQO. -/
lemma minimalGens_finite (U : Set α)
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop)) :
    (minimalGens U).Finite :=
  (isAntichain_minimalGens U).finite_of_wellQuasiOrdered hwqo

/-- In a well-quasi-order every element of a set dominates a minimal element of
that set (via well-foundedness of `<`). -/
lemma exists_minimalGen_le (U : Set α)
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    {x : α} (hx : x ∈ U) : ∃ g ∈ minimalGens U, g ≤ x := by
  obtain ⟨g, hg⟩ : ∃ g ∈ {y | y ∈ U ∧ y ≤ x}, ∀ z ∈ {y | y ∈ U ∧ y ≤ x}, ¬(z < g) := by
    convert (WellFounded.has_min _ {y | y ∈ U ∧ y ≤ x} ⟨x, hx, le_rfl⟩) using 1
    convert hwqo.wellFounded using 1
    grind +suggestions
  exact ⟨g, ⟨hg.1.1, fun z hz hz' => hg.2 z ⟨hz', hz.le.trans hg.1.2⟩ hz⟩, hg.1.2⟩

/-- An upper set of a well-quasi-order equals the up-set generated by its minimal
elements. -/
theorem mem_iff_exists_minimalGen (U : Set α)
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    (hU : IsUpperSet U) (x : α) :
    x ∈ U ↔ ∃ g ∈ minimalGens U, g ≤ x := by
  constructor
  · exact fun hx => exists_minimalGen_le U hwqo hx
  · exact fun ⟨g, hg, hgx⟩ => hU hgx (minimalGens_subset U hg)

/-- **Finite generation of upper sets.**  Abstractly this is the content of
Dickson's lemma / the Higman finite-basis property: in a well-quasi-order, every
upward-closed set is generated by a finite set of elements below it. -/
theorem exists_finite_generating_family
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    (U : Set α) (hU : IsUpperSet U) :
    ∃ G : Set α, G.Finite ∧ G ⊆ U ∧ ∀ x, x ∈ U ↔ ∃ g ∈ G, g ≤ x :=
  ⟨minimalGens U, minimalGens_finite U hwqo, minimalGens_subset U,
    fun x => mem_iff_exists_minimalGen U hwqo hU x⟩

/-- **Finite forbidden-obstruction characterization of lower sets.**  Abstractly
this is the content of the Robertson–Seymour corollary: in a well-quasi-order,
every downward-closed (minor-closed) set `S` is described by a finite family `B`
of "forbidden" elements, in the sense that `x ∈ S` iff no forbidden element lies
below `x`.  The family `B` is the set of minimal elements of the complement. -/
theorem exists_finite_forbidden_family
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    (S : Set α) (hS : IsLowerSet S) :
    ∃ B : Set α, B.Finite ∧ B ⊆ Sᶜ ∧ ∀ x, x ∈ S ↔ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬ b ≤ x := by
  obtain ⟨B, hB₁, hB₂, hB₃⟩ := exists_finite_generating_family hwqo Sᶜ hS.compl
  simp_all only [Set.subset_def, Set.mem_compl_iff]
  grind

/-- **Robertson–Seymour corollary, abstract form.**  If a class of combinatorial
objects (graphs, or `F_q`-representable matroids) is well-quasi-ordered by its
"minor" order, then every minor-closed property is characterized by a *finite*
set of forbidden minors.  This is exactly `exists_finite_forbidden_family`, stated
in the language of the mission. -/
theorem robertson_seymour_of_wqo
    (hwqo : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : α → α → Prop))
    (S : Set α) (hS : IsLowerSet S) :
    ∃ forbidden : Set α, forbidden.Finite ∧
      ∀ x, x ∈ S ↔ ∀ b ∈ forbidden, ¬ b ≤ x := by
  obtain ⟨B, hBfin, _, hB⟩ := exists_finite_forbidden_family hwqo S hS
  exact ⟨B, hBfin, hB⟩

/-! ## Concrete bridge: Dickson's lemma on `Fin k → ℕ`

We now instantiate the abstract engine on the exponent lattice `Fin k → ℕ`,
where `≤` is coordinatewise (equivalently monomial divisibility).  Mathlib
provides the instance `WellQuasiOrderedLE (Fin k → ℕ)`, so the abstract results
apply verbatim, yielding Dickson's lemma: every monomial-ideal-shaped upper set
is finitely generated. -/

/-- `ℕ` is well-quasi-ordered by `≤`. -/
theorem wqo_nat : WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : ℕ → ℕ → Prop) :=
  (inferInstance : WellQuasiOrderedLE ℕ).wqo

/-- The exponent lattice `Fin k → ℕ` is well-quasi-ordered by the coordinatewise
order — this is Dickson's lemma. -/
theorem wqo_fin_pi (k : ℕ) :
    WellQuasiOrdered ((· ≤ ·) : (Fin k → ℕ) → (Fin k → ℕ) → Prop) :=
  (inferInstance : WellQuasiOrderedLE (Fin k → ℕ)).wqo

/-- **Dickson's lemma, finite-generation form.**  Every upward-closed set of
exponent vectors in `ℕ^k` (equivalently, every monomial ideal) is finitely
generated by finitely many minimal exponent vectors. -/
theorem dickson (k : ℕ) (U : Set (Fin k → ℕ)) (hU : IsUpperSet U) :
    ∃ G : Set (Fin k → ℕ), G.Finite ∧ G ⊆ U ∧ ∀ x, x ∈ U ↔ ∃ g ∈ G, g ≤ x :=
  exists_finite_generating_family (wqo_fin_pi k) U hU

/-- Concrete forbidden-minor characterization on `ℕ` itself: every downward-closed
set of naturals is cut out by a finite forbidden set. -/
theorem forbidden_family_nat (S : Set ℕ) (hS : IsLowerSet S) :
    ∃ B : Set ℕ, B.Finite ∧ ∀ x, x ∈ S ↔ ∀ b ∈ B, ¬ b ≤ x := by
  obtain ⟨B, hBfin, _, hB⟩ := exists_finite_forbidden_family wqo_nat S hS
  exact ⟨B, hBfin, hB⟩

end WQOFiniteBasis
